newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB expected to signal Swiss rates should not rise.
newsitem.headline: SNB expected to signal Swiss rates should not rise.

text.p: Swiss currency and interest rate analysts believe the Swiss National Bank will send a signal to the market that it does not favour higher money market interest rates, but the question is when.
They say the timing could be tied to what results the SNB wants to achieve: preferably lower short-term rates and a gradual, long-term weakening in the Swiss franc.
"In our view, the SNB does not intend to tighten policy and does not at all want higher interest rates. On the contrary," CS Research analyst Michael Bernegger said.
"Sooner or later, the SNB will clarify this policy," he added in a market comment.

Swiss money market rates have risen since the SNB cut the discount rate on September 26 to 1.00 percent from 1.50 percent. The rise in short-term rates has roughly tracked the drop in the Swiss franc.
Tomorrow/next money was quoted at 1-11/16 percent on Wednesday. Banks quoted the rate at 1-1/4 to 1-1/2 percent in early October. By mid-October, the rate was back to around 1-1/2 percent.
The price of the three-month March Euroswiss contract traded on LIFFE has dropped back to mid-September levels, trading at 97.63 compared with a peak 98.32 on October 4.

The Swiss franc has touched 21-month lows against the dollar, and fallen by 4.4 percent against the mark since late August. Traders in short-term Swiss instruments have been speculating about the SNB's intentions and trade is nervous.
"We are seeing less and less people in the market. It looks like a market that has been mugged," said one EuroSwiss trader.

He said that traders were caught out when Swiss short-term rates rose in the spring, and surprised again when the SNB eased in September. Some traders may be interpreting the latest rise in Swiss short term rates as SNB-sanctioned.
But currency analyst Paul Lambert at Union Bank of Switzerland in London said the market is misreading the SNB.

"I think the whole year, the last 18 months people have been speculating rates are going up in Switzerland and they have been proved wrong... The market has taken the signs of more positive growth in Germany as a reason for the SNB to be cautious, and I think they are wrong," Lambert said.

He said the SNB had probably recognised that the problems of the weak Swiss economy and strong Swiss franc are unique. But the SNB might be reluctant to push too hard for lower interest rates for fear of causing a short-term speculative franc weakness, as opposed to a more desirable long-term drop.

Lambert said the SNB would probably prefer to see a gradual sustainable franc depreciation stemming from domestic capital exports, as opposed to a volatile franc outflow that would be more likely if big funds sold speculatively.
Speculative selling has also been a likely culprit behind the tightness in the Swiss money market. It causes short-term interest rates to rise, exactly what the SNB may not want.
"I think (the SNB doesn't) want to encourage shorting the Swiss franc," Lambert said.

Funds speculating that the franc will fall will borrow, or go short in Swiss francs and then sell them in the hope that further depreciation in the currency will net a gain when they have to repurchase the francs.
The question remains how and whether the SNB can encourage capital exports to weaken the franc on a long-term basis. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
